Script:


INTERVIEW WITH PIETER GROENEWALD


FULL TRANSCRIPT (with timecode)

00:00:01:14 - 00:00:34:11
Claire: Yesterday, a protest was held outside the US Embassy in Pretoria, attended by several hundred Afrikaans South Africans. The gathering expressed support for Donald Trump and his hardline stance against our government. It comes two weeks after Trump accused President Cyril Ramaphosa's administration, in his words, of confiscating land and treating certain classes of people very badly. He issued an executive order to deal with what he termed egregious actions by our government, and offered Afrikaners the chance to resettle in the US.

00:00:34:28 - 00:01:21:10
Lourensa: It's a diplomatic spat that's grown increasingly divisive, with our government saying it refuses to be bullied. But what are the likely consequences of Trump's position? We're joined now by Doctor Pieter Groenewald, Freedom Front Plus leader and minister in the Government of National Unity. Minister, before we start, let's take a look at President Cyril Ramaphosa's response on X to the executive order issued by President Donald Trump. Ramaphosa said South Africa is a constitutional democracy that is deeply rooted in the rule of law, justice and equality. South Africa, like the United States of America and other countries, has always had expropriation laws that balance the need for public usage of land and the protection of rights of property owners. Minister, what is the Freedom Front Plus's stance? Is land being confiscated left and right in South Africa?

00:01:21:28 - 00:02:13:02
Groenewald: It is true that we have always had an expropriation act, but this one is different. The difference is that this expropriation act provides for expropriation without compensation. It was not in the previous act. So that is a huge difference. And the fact of the matter is, of course, it's known all over South Africa that there is illegal invasion of land. And I said it in Parliament, there are numerous examples where there was actually illegal invasion. So that's an inconvenient truth of South Africa. And the problem the government has is that we're in 2025. On social media, if those incidents happen, then everybody in the world can see it.

00:02:13:05 - 00:02:28:00
Lourensa: But Minister, we still have a Constitution where property right is guaranteed. Article 25 provides for expropriation, does not provide for expropriation without compensation. So if these laws are tested in court, will it not be found unconstitutional?

00:02:28:21 - 00:03:24:05
Groenewald: No. Well, it depends on how you want to see it. I mean, expropriation without compensation as far as the Freedom Front Plus is concerned, is exactly unconstitutional. Section 25 of the Constitution is quite clear. It says, yes, you can have expropriation, but there must be compensation that is fair and equitable. Now, section 12 of the new act provides in certain circumstances for expropriation without compensation. And we say that that is unconstitutional. Remember in 2017, 2018, around about 2019, those years, there was a motion in Parliament, trying to amend section 25 of the Constitution. We did not succeed because the ANC could not get the two thirds majority. So why did they want to change it if it was not necessary? That's actually proof that they know they are wrong.

00:03:24:10 - 00:03:49:19
Lourensa: Minister, another part of the executive order states that certain classes of people are being treated very badly in this country. If we look at the protests that happened yesterday at the United States Embassy, would it not amplify the message of some of these groups to say that if you are concerned about crime in South Africa, if you are concerned about economic policies that threaten property rights, these policies and crime will have a detrimental effect on all South Africans, not just certain groups?

00:03:50:10 - 00:04:50:09
Groenewald: It depends. Because let's take black economic empowerment that is for a specific group. I as a white person in South Africa cannot deal in, can I say, the benefits of black economic empowerment. And I must put it very clearly. There are black, can I say leaders and also commentators who is also confirming that black economic empowerment does not favour the poor in South Africa. When you're a white student and you want to apply for a loan, or if you want to study certain degrees in universities because you're white, they say you do not qualify. Now that for me is discrimination. Yes, and I know section 32 of the Constitution provides that there can be justifiable discrimination. But listen, they acknowledge that it is discrimination. But we must move away from that.

00:04:50:11 - 00:04:59:12
Lourensa: Minister, do you think this is about land confiscation and the expropriation law, or do you think we are punished for our stance and taking Israel to the International Criminal Court?

00:04:59:21 - 00:05:50:00
Groenewald: Well, surely Israel plays quite a role. I do believe that the expropriation is not the main reason why we have this can I say presidential executive order, but he referred to South Africa and of course, as a president, he will use any argument to justify his decision. Therefore, yes, it's order, or can I say a punishment for what happened with the Israel situation. Also the Iran situation, which they referred to and therefore and we can even go further, if we look at the international can I say policy of the ANC, of who their friends are, then, of course, that is why I think President Trump put out this executive order.

00:05:50:15 - 00:06:08:12
Lourensa: So if it's important for our government to take a principled stance with regard to Israel, should our government also then clearly communicate what those consequences will be? Because it is, as you say, President Donald Trump of the United States saying there will be consequences to our stance regarding Israel, our friendship with Iran, etc..

00:06:08:25 - 00:06:32:27
Groenewald: I already said in Parliament, of course it's going to have consequences. And I said, we must solve these problems and therefore we must have communication with the government in Washington, but we must put up in front of us even the inconvenient truths, and then we must ask each other, how are we going to solve it? What are you...?

00:06:32:29 - 00:06:38:01
Lourensa: But Minister, you are in government. How are we going to solve this? Who are we sending to speak to leaders in Washington?

00:06:38:09 - 00:07:47:19
Groenewald: Well, yes, you're quite right. I'm part of the GNU. Therefore, I said that, go to Washington. Ask them exactly how do they see the problems, and how do they want it to be solved. And then we can put our view forward. But we cannot go to Washington and don't put the inconvenient truth on the table. And that's the problem I have. Therefore, I foresee I won't be part of the delegation, because if I have to go there, I will put the inconvenient truth on the table. Like illegal land invasion and occupation. We must deal with that matter. I mean, there are numerous cases where, I mean, farmers are actually threatened. I have a specific case in Wepener where the illegal invader actually put a firearm against his forehead and said, what can you do? And when he went to the police for protection, they didn't want to listen to him. That is totally unacceptable. And we must remember, the police is actually an arm of the executive of the government. Therefore, they are complicit, allowing these illegal land invasions.

00:07:47:29 - 00:08:04:14
Lourensa: But is it not a slippery slope to ask foreign countries to intervene in domestic matters? You yourself said that we should take these matters to the police. The National Prosecuting Authority should take, should play its role as well. We have internal structures to deal with this. Is it really necessary for a foreign country to get involved?

00:08:04:21 - 00:08:28:26
Groenewald: It's not supposed to be necessary for foreign countries to be involved. But as you said, it's supposed to deal with the matter. The police is supposed to see that you are protected, but they don't do it. Now, let's go back in the history. I mean, when the ANC, before they were the government, they went all over the world and asked countries to put sanctions against South Africa for their cause.

00:08:28:28 - 00:08:33:16
Lourensa: But are you saying what white people are experiencing in South Africa at the moment can be compared to apartheid?

00:08:33:22 - 00:09:16:13
Groenewald: No, I don't say that. But this is a specific problem, what white people are experiencing in South Africa, whether you like it or not. Because let's go to the illegal land invasion. You can go and look, it's actually white property owners that are affected by this invasion. I am not aware of any land invasion where the land owner was a black person, and I say we must not shy away talking about black and white in South Africa. It's a reality. But I always say we must respect each other and also ensure that we deal with our problems in a respectful way.

00:09:16:15 - 00:09:24:03
Lourensa: What will be the economic consequences if we are kicked out of Agoa? And if tariffs are placed on South African goods being exported to the US?

00:09:24:26 - 00:10:27:14
Groenewald: The results will be enormously detrimental to South Africa, specifically the economy. If you're referring to Agoa, firstly we're talking about Agoa alone, we talk about, say, in the vicinity of R400 billion that will be affected because it's about trade in this matter. And the main sectors that will be affected, the biggest effect will be on our vehicle manufacturing in South Africa. Then even chemicals like Sasol. And then thirdly, it will be the agricultural sector. But the main thing is we're going to lose quite a lot of people going to lose their jobs. If we refer to the USAID alone, in the health sector, they're talking about almost 15,000 jobs that will be lost because only of that. So you can imagine that there are speculation, of course, but they say that up to 500,000 people can lose their jobs because of Agoa.

00:10:27:21 - 00:10:45:21
Lourensa: Minister Pieter Groenewald, thank you very much. If you have thoughts on this story or any of the others covered in tonight's show, please join the online conversation.
